title: How does Kafka balance load across consumers in a group, and what happens on join/failure (rebalancing)?
shortTitle: How Kafka balances load across consumers and handles join/failure (rebalancing)

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka balances load across a consumer group by distributing the topic's partitions among the group's consumers so that each consumer owns a roughly equal share, with every partition owned by exactly one consumer. When the group membership changes — a consumer joins, leaves gracefully, or fails to send heartbeats — the group coordinator initiates a rebalance, which recomputes and redistributes partition ownership. Classic eager rebalancing revokes all partitions and reassigns them, briefly pausing consumption, while cooperative incremental rebalancing moves only the partitions that must change, minimizing disruption.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture a team of clerks at National Bank of India sharing stacks of transaction forms. The supervisor splits the stacks evenly so everyone has about the same workload. If a new clerk joins, the supervisor takes a few stacks from the busy clerks and hands them over. If a clerk goes home sick without telling anyone and stops responding, the supervisor notices the silence, takes that clerk's stacks, and shares them among the remaining clerks so no form is left unprocessed. This reshuffling is the rebalance.
s1_definition.oneliner: Kafka spreads partitions evenly across consumers, and a rebalance redistributes them whenever a consumer joins or fails.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka balances load across a consumer group by distributing the topic's partitions among the group's consumers so that each consumer owns a roughly equal share, with every partition owned by exactly one consumer. When the group membership changes — a consumer joins, leaves gracefully, or fails to send heartbeats — the group coordinator initiates a rebalance, which recomputes and redistributes partition ownership. Classic eager rebalancing revokes all partitions and reassigns them, briefly pausing consumption, while cooperative incremental rebalancing moves only the partitions that must change, minimizing disruption.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture a team of clerks at National Bank of India sharing stacks of transaction forms. The supervisor splits the stacks evenly so everyone has about the same workload. If a new clerk joins, the supervisor takes a few stacks from the busy clerks and hands them over. If a clerk goes home sick without telling anyone and stops responding, the supervisor notices the silence, takes that clerk's stacks, and shares them among the remaining clerks so no form is left unprocessed. This reshuffling is the rebalance.

**One line to remember:** Kafka spreads partitions evenly across consumers, and a rebalance redistributes them whenever a consumer joins or fails.

sections.s2_technical:
Load balancing in Kafka means fair distribution of partitions. The group coordinator and the elected group leader compute an assignment using the configured `partition.assignment.strategy`. The RangeAssignor divides partitions into contiguous ranges, the RoundRobinAssignor spreads them one by one for even distribution, and the StickyAssignor and CooperativeStickyAssignor keep assignments stable across rebalances to avoid unnecessary movement. The goal is that each consumer owns about the same number of partitions so the processing load is even. Because a partition is the unit of parallelism, true load balancing requires enough partitions — more partitions than consumers lets you add consumers later for more throughput.

Heartbeats keep the coordinator informed that consumers are alive. Each consumer sends a heartbeat on a background thread every `heartbeat.interval.ms`. If the coordinator does not hear from a consumer within `session.timeout.ms`, it declares that consumer dead and starts a rebalance. There is also `max.poll.interval.ms`: if a consumer takes too long between calls to poll, usually because processing a batch is stuck, the coordinator assumes the consumer is unhealthy and removes it. Tuning these three values is how you balance fast failure detection against false eviction of slow-but-healthy consumers.

A rebalance is the process of redistributing partitions. In the classic eager protocol, every consumer revokes all its partitions, the leader computes a fresh assignment, and consumers receive their new partitions. This is simple but causes a stop-the-world pause where no partition is consumed, which hurts latency-sensitive systems. The cooperative incremental protocol, now the recommended default via CooperativeStickyAssignor, performs the rebalance in two phases: consumers only revoke the specific partitions that need to move to another consumer, keeping the rest flowing. This dramatically reduces the pause.

Three events trigger a rebalance. A consumer joining the group — for example a new service instance scaling up — causes the coordinator to take some partitions from existing consumers and give them to the newcomer. A consumer leaving gracefully — a clean shutdown that sends a LeaveGroup request — lets the coordinator immediately reassign its partitions. A consumer failing — crashing or getting stuck so heartbeats stop — causes the coordinator to detect the timeout and reassign the dead consumer's partitions to the survivors.

Offset handling matters during rebalance. Before a consumer gives up a partition, it should commit its current offset so the new owner resumes from the right place; otherwise the new owner may reprocess or, with bad configuration, skip records. In Spring Kafka you can hook `ConsumerRebalanceListener` callbacks, `onPartitionsRevoked` to commit offsets and `onPartitionsAssigned` to initialize state, to make rebalances clean. Static group membership via `group.instance.id` can also avoid rebalances during brief restarts by letting a returning consumer reclaim its previous partitions.

The senior-level nuance is that rebalances are necessary but costly, so you minimize unnecessary ones. Use the cooperative sticky assignor to avoid stop-the-world pauses, set `max.poll.records` and processing time so you never exceed `max.poll.interval.ms`, use static membership for rolling restarts, and monitor rebalance frequency. Frequent rebalances usually signal slow processing or misconfigured timeouts, and they directly cause consumer lag and duplicate processing.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs several instances of its transaction processor and must keep load even as instances scale up and occasionally crash.

Problem 1 — At peak the bank adds more processor instances to handle load, and the existing instances must give up some partitions so the new instance gets work. This is exactly a rebalance triggered by a consumer joining.

Problem 2 — An instance occasionally crashes during a deployment, and its partitions must be picked up by the survivors within seconds so transactions are not stuck. This is exactly a rebalance triggered by a failure detected through missed heartbeats.

Problem 3 — During the shuffle, the instance giving up a partition must commit its offset first so the new owner resumes at the right record, with no skipped or doubly-counted transactions. This is exactly the revoke-then-commit behavior of a clean rebalance.

The mini-project simulates a rebalancing processor group. We build a `Txn` domain object, a `PartitionLog` tracking a committed offset, a `Rebalancer` that evenly assigns partitions and commits offsets on revoke, and a `ProcessorGroup` that can add and fail consumers. The demo starts two instances, scales to three on join, then fails one, logging the balanced assignment and the offset commits at each step.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a processor group for the topic transactions with 6 partitions, each already processed up to some committed offset.

Step 1 — proc-1 joins. The group has one consumer, so it owns all 6 partitions. Before any reassignment, the rebalancer commits each partition's offset so handover is clean.

Step 2 — proc-2 joins, triggering a rebalance. The rebalancer commits offsets on the partitions being moved, then assigns evenly: proc-1 owns 3 partitions and proc-2 owns 3 partitions. The load is now balanced across two instances.

Step 3 — proc-3 joins at peak. Another rebalance occurs. Offsets are committed on revoke, and the assignment becomes 2 partitions each for proc-1, proc-2, proc-3. The load is perfectly even, and throughput increased because a third instance now shares the work.

Step 4 — proc-2 crashes and stops sending heartbeats. After the session timeout, the coordinator treats it as failed and triggers a rebalance. Offsets are committed, proc-2 is removed, and its partitions are redistributed to the survivors: proc-1 and proc-3 now own 3 partitions each. No partition is left unowned, so transaction processing continues without loss.

Step 5 — Because every revoke committed the offset first, each new owner resumes from the correct record. The logs show the balanced assignments and the offset commits at each rebalance, proving load stays even and no transaction is skipped or double-counted.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Topic transactions (P0..P5)   |   Group txn-processors
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  START: proc-1          → owns P0..P5 (all, unbalanced)
    │ proc-2 joins → REBALANCE (commit offsets on revoke)
    ▼
  proc-1 → P0,P2,P4      proc-2 → P1,P3,P5     (balanced 3+3)
    │ proc-3 joins → REBALANCE
    ▼
  proc-1 → P0,P3   proc-2 → P1,P4   proc-3 → P2,P5   (balanced 2+2+2)
    │ proc-2 FAILS (missed heartbeats) → REBALANCE
    ▼
  proc-1 → P0,P2,P4      proc-3 → P1,P3,P5     (survivors take over 3+3)

  Each REBALANCE: revoke → commit offset → reassign → resume at committed offset
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka balances load across a consumer group by distributing the topic's partitions evenly among the group's consumers, with every partition owned by exactly one consumer. The group coordinator and the elected group leader compute the assignment using a strategy like round-robin or, better, the cooperative-sticky assignor, aiming for each consumer to own roughly the same number of partitions. Because a partition is the unit of parallelism, true load balancing depends on having enough partitions, which is why I provision partitions with headroom for scaling.

A rebalance is how Kafka redistributes partitions when group membership changes, and three events trigger it. When a consumer joins, such as a new service instance scaling up, the coordinator takes some partitions from existing consumers and gives them to the newcomer. When a consumer leaves gracefully, it sends a LeaveGroup request and its partitions are reassigned immediately. When a consumer fails — crashing or getting stuck so its heartbeats stop arriving within the session timeout — the coordinator declares it dead and redistributes its partitions to the survivors.

Rebalances come in two flavors. The classic eager protocol revokes all partitions and reassigns them, causing a brief stop-the-world pause. The cooperative incremental protocol, which I prefer, only moves the partitions that actually need to change owner, keeping the rest flowing and minimizing disruption. During any rebalance, the consumer giving up a partition commits its offset first, so the new owner resumes at exactly the right record with no skipped or double-counted transactions.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, the transaction processor runs as an auto-scaled consumer group. When we add instances at peak, a rebalance evenly redistributes the partitions; when an instance crashes during a deployment, the survivors pick up its partitions within seconds. The senior point I always make is that rebalances are necessary but costly, so I minimize unnecessary ones by using the cooperative sticky assignor, tuning max.poll.interval.ms so slow processing does not cause false evictions, using static group membership for rolling restarts, and monitoring rebalance frequency, because frequent rebalances are a red flag for lag and duplicate processing.

---

keyPoints: Consumer group: set of consumers sharing topic partitions
Each partition assigned to exactly one consumer in a group
Rebalancing: partition reassignment when consumers join/leave
